Native to subtropical rainforest gullies of coastal New South Wales and southeast Queensland, this glossy-leaved tree contains one of the highest natural concentrations of anethole of any plant, giving the dried, ground leaf an intensely sweet licorice-anise flavor. Use the dried leaf in baking, fruit desserts, herbal tea blends, and as a striking substitute anywhere star anise or fennel seed is called for; it can be clipped and kept as a large shrub in gardens where space is limited.

planting.note: Plant rooted divisions or cuttings in spring in gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun to light shade, replicating the rocky Andean slopes of Peru, Bolivia, and Ecuador where muña grows wild.

This shrubby mint relative has hairy, serrated, intensely camphor-mint-scented leaves traditionally added to cooking beans and potatoes to reduce flatulence and brewed as a digestive tea. Harvest leafy stems just before flowering for the strongest aroma, and use fresh or air-dried in place of huacatay or regular mint in Peruvian stews and ceviche marinades.
sources: Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity (Ark of Taste)

planting.note: Establish rooted cuttings in spring under the dappled shade of taller trees, since this caffeinated Amazonian holly is naturally an understory species requiring humid, warm, tropical conditions with well-drained but consistently moist soil.

directions: Establish rooted cuttings in spring under the dappled shade of taller trees, since this caffeinated Amazonian holly is naturally an understory species requiring humid, warm, tropical conditions with well-drained but consistently moist soil. Traditionally grown alongside cacao and coffee in Kichwa agroforestry plots of Ecuador, guayusa produces glossy, elongated leaves that are harvested young, lightly toasted or sun-dried, and steeped into a stimulating morning tea richer in caffeine than yerba mate. Light harvesting can begin about a year after planting, with full annual yields developing as the tree matures over roughly five years.

planting.note: Transplant young trees in spring into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; check local regulations before planting, since molle is classified as invasive or restricted in parts of California and the desert Southwest.

directions: Transplant young trees in spring into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; this fast-growing, drought-tolerant evergreen from the Peruvian Andes develops graceful, weeping, willow-like branches and clusters of small berries that ripen from green to bright rose-pink. The dried berries are sold commercially as pink peppercorns and add a fruity, mildly resinous heat to pepper blends, sauces, and infused oils, though botanically the tree is unrelated to true pepper (Piper nigrum). Handle fresh fruit and sap with care, as some people develop mild skin or respiratory irritation, and check local regulations before planting, since molle is classified as invasive or restricted in parts of California and the desert Southwest.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products

planting.note: Soak seed in freshly boiled water overnight to soften its hard coat, sow into acidic, sandy, low-fertility soil, and grow seedlings on for about two months before transplanting into their permanent full-sun position.

Rooibos is a fine-needled legume shrub found only in South Africa's Cederberg mountains, where hot dry summers and cool wet winters shape its narrow native range. Harvested stems are cut, bruised, and left to oxidize before drying, turning the leaves the deep red-brown that gives the naturally caffeine-free, sweetly earthy tea its color and name.
